source_text: XXXI. Doctores autem illi ex hac sua concursus divini explicatione, putant se facile ostendere posse, quomodo cum actuum humanorum libertate concursus ille conciliari possit. Cum enim duplex tribui soleat voluntati libertas, una scilicet, quoad exercitium actus, & altera quoad ejus specificationem, neutri quicquam praejudicat concursus divinus ita explicatus. Non priori quae est quoad exercitium, quandoquidem iste concursus necessitatem agendi voluntati non imponit: si quidem voluntas non operatur quia Deus operatur, sed potius e converso ideo Deus operatur, quia Voluntas operatur; quamvis alioqui in eodem momento temporis & naturae, Deus & Voluntas operari incipiant. Quod Scholasticis vocibus sic exprimunt, voluntatem prius natura operari quam Deum, non prioritate instantis in quo, sed a quo.
english: These teachers believe that their account of divine concurrence lets them show easily how it can be reconciled with the freedom of human acts.

Two kinds of freedom are usually ascribed to the will: freedom as to the exercise of the act and freedom as to its specification. Concurrence understood in their way takes nothing from either. It does not impair freedom of exercise, since it lays no necessity of acting on the will. The will does not act because God acts; rather, God acts because the will acts, even though God and the will begin to act at the same moment of time and of nature. In the language of the Schools they put it this way: the will acts prior by nature to God, not with the priority of the instant 'in which' but of the instant 'from which'.

source_text: XXXII. Quamvis vero Voluntas, sine Deo concurrente, nihil omnino possit, ex lege tamen a Deo, dum liberam illam condidit, constituta, concursus ille semper ipsi praesto est, quia Deus voluit, & ab aeterno decrevit ad omne opus liberae voluntatis concurrere, quando ad operandum ipsa se determinaverit. Nec minus eadem Voluntas libera est quoad actus sui specificationem. Quod enim voluntas bene vel male agit, istud potius fugit quam appetit, ex vi quadam divini concursus non procedit, sed ex propria Voluntatis determinatione, quae ad hujus potius quam alterius speciei actionem edendam, concursu divino ex se indifferenti libere utitur.
english: The will can do nothing at all without God's concurrence. Yet under the law God laid down when he made it free, that concurrence is always ready for it, because God willed, and decreed from eternity, to concur in every work of the free will once the will has determined itself to act.

The will is no less free as to the specification of its act. Whether it acts well or badly, whether it shuns a thing rather than seeks it, does not come from any force in the divine concurrence but from the will's own determination. In producing an action of this kind rather than that, the will freely makes use of God's concurrence, which of itself is indifferent.

source_text: XXXIII. Quod ad Reformatos attinet, qui in Belgio Remonstrantes dicuntur, sive Arminiani, non alium Dei concursum cum causis secundis agnoscunt quam illum generalem atque indifferentem, & qui a causae secundae concursu determinetur. Id videre est apud Jacobum Arminium, a quo reliqui omnes denominantur. Nam contra Perkinsum disputans, non tantum affirmat concursum illum Dei ex se indifferentem esse, sed eum quoque nihil conferre voluntati creaturae, quo ad agendum vel inclinetur, vel juvetur, vel confortetur, & voluntatem creatam habere Dei concursum in potestate sua, priusquam operetur, paratum sibi & expositum. In Antiperkinso pag. 733. Quibus similia docent Grevinchovius contra Amesium sect. 32. pag. 368. Et Corvinus contra Tilenum cap. 9. pag. 354.
english: Among the Reformed, those in the Netherlands called Remonstrants or Arminians acknowledge no concurrence of God with secondary causes other than the general, indifferent one that is determined by the concurrence of the secondary cause.

This can be seen in Jacobus Arminius, after whom all the rest are named. Arguing against Perkins, he not only asserts that this concurrence of God is indifferent in itself, but also that it 'contributes nothing to the creature's will by which it is inclined, helped or strengthened to act', and that 'the created will has God's concurrence in its own power before it acts, ready and laid out for it' (Antiperkinsus, p. 733). Grevinchovius teaches much the same against Ames (section 32, p. 368), and Corvinus against Tilenus (chapter 9, p. 354).

source_text: XXXIV. Sed & ex iis Reformatis qui Dordracenae Synodo subscribunt, nonnulli hac in parte idem sentire videntur cum Molinistis & Remonstrantibus, neque alium Dei generalem cum causis secundis concursum agnoscere, quam simultaneum, atque indifferentem, quo Deus non in causam ipsam, sed in actum ejus cum ipsa influat, quique causam secundam ad hanc, vel illam actus speciem non determinet, sed a causa secunda pro illius natura, aut etiam libertate, varie modificetur.
english: Even among the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort, some seem to agree on this point with the Molinists and the Remonstrants.

They recognize no general concurrence of God with secondary causes other than a simultaneous and indifferent one. By it God acts not on the cause itself but, together with the cause, on its act. It does not determine the secondary cause to one kind of act or another; instead the secondary cause shapes it in various ways according to its nature, or even its freedom.

source_text: XXXV. Haec saltem est procul omni dubio sententia Roberti Baronii Scoti, dum viveret in Academia Abredonensi Theologiae Professoris, ut videre est in ejus Metaphysica ad Theologiae usum accommodata; ubi de Dei concursu, adeoque de ejus cum arbitrii nostri libertate concordia, idem omnino se sentire profitetur cum Fonseca & Suarezio, nempe concursum illum ex se indifferentem esse, & a causa secunda ad certam actionis speciem determinari: neque opus esse ut Deus causas secundas praemoveat, sed sufficere ut simul cum iis in earum effectus & actiones influat: adeoque Dei concursum & influxum revera non aliud esse quam ipsam causae secundae actionem, in quantum a prima causa, simul cum secunda, esse suum accipit, & ab ea dependet. Sectione octava, Disp. 3. De concursu seu cooperatione Dei.
english: This at any rate is beyond all doubt the view of the Scot Robert Baron, professor of theology at the University of Aberdeen during his lifetime, as can be seen in his Metaphysics adapted to the use of theology.

On God's concurrence, and so on its agreement with the freedom of our choice, he declares that he holds exactly the same as Fonseca and Suárez. The concurrence is indifferent in itself and is determined by the secondary cause to a particular kind of action. God has no need to premove secondary causes; it is enough that he acts together with them on their effects and actions. God's concurrence and influence is thus in reality nothing other than the secondary cause's action itself, insofar as that action receives its being from the first cause together with the second and depends on it (Section 8, Disputation 3, 'On the concurrence or cooperation of God').

source_text: XXXVI. Nec multum abesse videtur ab ista Sententia Joannes Strangius Scotus, etiam ipse & in Academia Glasguensi Professor. Quanquam enim censeat * actionem ad quam Deus & creatura simul concurrunt, prius natura esse a Deo, quam a creatura; & influxum Dei in actionem illam, esse natura priorem quam influxum creaturae; & praeterea neget † Deum concurrere tantum generali influxu; ut sol eodem modo concurrit ad generationem hominis & equi: sed influxum Dei statuat specialem ad speciales effectus, prout specie distinguuntur, non moraliter, sed Physice; multis tamen contendit & probat ad omnes & singulos creaturarum actus, necessariam non esse illam Dei praemotionem, & praedeterminationem, quam Thomae Schola tuetur & defendit. * De voluntate & actionibus Dei circa peccatum lib. cap. 11. † Lib. 2. cap. 3.
english: The Scot John Strang, himself also a professor, at the University of Glasgow, does not seem far from this view.

He holds that the action in which God and the creature concur comes from God prior by nature to its coming from the creature, and that God's influence on that action is prior by nature to the creature's influence (De voluntate et actionibus Dei circa peccatum, book not numbered in the print, chapter 11). He also denies that God concurs only by a general influence, as the sun concurs in the same way in generating a man and a horse (book 2, chapter 3); he posits a special influence of God for special effects, as these differ in kind, and that physically, not morally. Even so, he argues at length, and proves, that the premotion and predetermination of God which the school of Thomas maintains and defends is not necessary for each and every act of creatures.

source_text: XXXVII. Per praemotionem autem & praedeterminationem illam declarat se intelligere actionem Dei, qua Deus ciet & applicat secundam causam ad agendum, adeoque prius natura & ratione quam creatura operetur, eam realiter & efficaciter movet ad singulas ejus actiones; agens & faciens ut creatura agat & faciat quicquid illa agit & facit: ita ut sine hac Dei praemotione nihil prorsus possit agere creatura; illa vero posita, impossibile sit in sensu composito causam secundam illud non agere ad quod a causa prima praemovetur. Ejusmodi praemotionem & praedeterminationem agnoscit quidem ille a Deo adhiberi ad opera gratiae, & ad plurimas alias Voluntatis operationes, nempe quandocunque ipsi libet & opus est: negat tamen eam ad communem Dei concursum spectare, aut universe adhiberi ad omnes creaturarum actiones, praesertim eas quibus peccatum necessario annexum est. Lib. 2. cap. 4. sub finem.
english: By that premotion and predetermination, he explains, he means the action by which God stirs and applies the secondary cause to act. Prior by nature and by reason to the creature's acting, God really and efficaciously moves it to each of its actions, acting and bringing it about that the creature acts and does whatever it acts and does. Without this premotion of God the creature can do nothing whatever; once it is given, it is impossible in the composite sense for the secondary cause not to do what the first cause premoves it to.

Strang grants that God does use premotion and predetermination of this kind for the works of grace and for very many other operations of the will, whenever he pleases and there is need. But he denies that it belongs to God's common concurrence or is applied across the board to all the actions of creatures, especially those to which sin is necessarily attached (book 2, chapter 4, near the end).

source_text: XXXVIII. Ut autem sic sentiat, eo praecipue se moveri testatur, quod si ad omnes peccati actiones Deus necessario diabolos hominesque impios determinaret, inde sequi existimat peccata nostra Deo merito imputari posse: qua etiam ratione se maxime permotum affirmat Robertus Baronius ille supra citatus.
english: Strang says he holds this view chiefly because, if God necessarily determined devils and wicked men to every action of sin, it would follow, in his judgment, that our sins could rightly be charged to God.
Robert Baron, cited above, says this was the reason that weighed most with him as well.

source_text: XXXIX. Sed uterque praeterea istam praedeterminationem eo nomine rejiciendam putat quod libertati Voluntatis officit, nec videtur cum ea conciliari posse. * Distinguit tamen Strangius inter libertatem latius acceptam quae Voluntati essentialis est, & quae reperitur in quolibet actu qui fit sponte & cum ratione; & inter libertatem strictiore sensu sumptam, quae consistit in quadam agentis indifferentia, & Voluntati respectu plerorumque ipsius actuum competit. Priorem illam libertatem non evertit, juxta ipsum, divina praemotio & praedeterminatio, qua Deus homines suaviter movet, & prout creaturae intelligenti consentaneum est: sed tamen cum strictiore ista libertate consistere nequit, ut quae posita sit in indifferentia, cum qua pugnat antecedens quaevis determinatio, & quae in Voluntatis ipsius potestate non sit. Quomodo vero tali libertati nihil noceat concursus ille Dei simultaneus, & qui semper praesto est creatae Voluntati, superius expositum fuit. Nec Theologi isti eum cum stricte dicta voluntatis libertate aliter conciliant quam Scholae Romanae Doctores. * Strangius de Voluntat. Dei circa peccatum, lib. 2. cap. 8.
english: Both men also hold that this predetermination should be rejected because it damages the freedom of the will and does not seem capable of being reconciled with it.

Strang does, however, distinguish two senses of freedom (De voluntate Dei circa peccatum, book 2, chapter 8). Freedom in the broader sense is essential to the will and is found in any act done willingly and with reason. Freedom in the stricter sense consists in a certain indifference on the agent's part and belongs to the will with respect to most of its acts. On his view, the divine premotion and predetermination by which God moves human beings gently, in a way suited to an intelligent creature, does not overturn the first kind of freedom. It cannot, however, coexist with the stricter kind, since that freedom lies in indifference, which any prior determination not within the will's own power contradicts.

How God's simultaneous concurrence, always ready for the created will, does no harm to freedom of that kind has been explained above. These theologians reconcile it with freedom in the strict sense in just the same way as the teachers of the Roman School.

source_text: XL. Plurimi tamen inter Theologos Reformatos censent cum Thomae Schola, Deum non solum ad singulos creaturarum actus simul cum iis concurrere atque cooperari, sed etiam creaturas nihil agere posse, nisi ad hos & illos actus efficaciter a Deo praemoveantur & praedeterminentur: idque locum habere tam in causis liberis quam in necessariis, & tam in malis actibus quam in bonis; licet Deus non moveat, neque praedeterminet ad malitiam & pravitatem actus, sed tantum ad illud quod est in eo positivum & naturaliter bonum. Ac quemadmodum ex eorum sententia causa secunda sine tali praedeterminatione nihil agere & operari potest, ita quoque illa supposita, impossibile est eam non agere atque operari.
english: Very many Reformed theologians, however, side with the school of Thomas. They hold that God not only concurs and cooperates with creatures in each of their acts, but that creatures can do nothing unless God efficaciously premoves and predetermines them to this act or that.

This holds, they say, for free causes as much as for necessary ones, and for evil acts as much as for good ones, although God does not move or predetermine to the malice and depravity of the act, only to what is positive and naturally good in it. And just as on their view the secondary cause can do or perform nothing without such predetermination, so too, once it is given, the cause cannot fail to act and perform.

source_text: XLI. Ejusmodi causarum secundarum praemotionem & praedeterminationem, ac praecipue humanae voluntatis, admittendam statuit Gul. Amesius; quia alioquin, ipsius judicio, tolletur subordinatio causae primae & causarum secundarum in suis operationibus. Subtrahentur dominio providentiae, & gubernationi Dei efficaci, operationes omnes Voluntatis humanae. Homo non subditus, sed socius Dei erit. Imo Deus pendebit ex hominis nutu, etiam in iis quae praecipuam rationem habent in totius mundi procuratione. Nec homo dicere debebit, Si Deus voluerit faciam hoc aut illud; sed potius Deus dicere debebit, Si homo voluerit faciam hoc aut illud. In Bellarmino Enervato tomo quarto, libro quarto, capite secundo.
english: William Ames holds that premotion and predetermination of this kind must be admitted for secondary causes, and above all for the human will. Otherwise, in his judgment, the subordination of secondary causes to the first cause in their operations would be done away with.

Every operation of the human will would be removed from the rule of providence and from God's efficacious government. Man would be God's partner rather than his subject. Indeed God would hang on man's nod even in matters that weigh most in governing the whole world. Man would no longer have to say, 'If God wills, I shall do this or that'; rather God would have to say, 'If man wills, I shall do this or that' (Bellarminus enervatus, tome 4, book 4, chapter 2).

source_text: XLII. In eadem sententia est Samuel Retorfortis Scotus, ante paucos annos in Academia Andreapolitana Theologiae Professor. Nam Concursum Dei ex se Generalem, & indifferentem, & qui a causae secundae concursu determinatur, tanquam commentitium & impium pluribus argumentis refutat. Quippe, ut ipse existimat, istiusmodi concursus Deo injuriosus est; quoniam Deo libertatem in decernendo eripit, & infert foedam Dei a creaturae suae lubrico nutu dependentiam, quandoquidem supponit Deum a creatura, non vero creaturam a Deo determinari. Praeterea tollit usum precum illarum quibus a Deo petimus, ut corda nostra, & aliorum flectat, prout saluti nostrae & illorum expedit: Siquidem id fieri non potest, nisi per operationem qua Deus Voluntates hominum determinet. Et ob eandem rationem frustra gratiae Deo agerentur de bonis procuratis per agentia libera. Nec etiam erit a Deo Copia divitiarum quae obveniunt hominibus actibus liberis mercandi. Et denique neganda erit particularis Dei providentia, quam Scriptura tam saepe commendat. De divina Providentia cap. 25.
english: The Scot Samuel Rutherford, who was professor of theology at the University of St Andrews a few years ago, holds the same view. He attacks with many arguments, as fictitious and impious, a concurrence of God that is general and indifferent in itself and is determined by the concurrence of the secondary cause.

In his judgment such a concurrence wrongs God. It robs God of freedom in his decrees and makes God shamefully dependent on the fickle nod of his creature, since it supposes that God is determined by the creature rather than the creature by God. It also removes the point of the prayers in which we ask God to bend our hearts and the hearts of others as our salvation and theirs requires, for that cannot happen except through an operation by which God determines human wills. For the same reason it would be pointless to thank God for good things obtained through free agents. Nor would the wealth that comes to people through their free acts of trade be from God. Finally, God's particular providence, which Scripture so often commends, would have to be denied (De divina providentia, chapter 25).

source_text: XLIII. In Exercitationibus autem Apologeticis pro divina gratia asserit, Deum in omnibus actibus tum naturae, tum gratiae, voluntatem determinare per impulsum vere realem ad modum causae Physicae; quanquam subjungit litem praecipuam non esse an praedeterminatio ista Physica dicenda sit, sed an Deus actus liberos praedeterminet indeclinabiliter: Quaestio enim, inquit, est, Annon ita moveat voluntatem Deus, ut sub illa motione non possit mota non permoveri, vel annon Actio Dei in Voluntatem ita ipsam flectat, ut non possit non libere se flectere illuc quo Deus ipsam inclinat: nos vero ex Scripturis probamus necessitationem Voluntatis a Dei motione qua indeclinabiliter permoveatur. Quod si quis concedat, addit se Physicae praedeterminationi valedicere paratum esse: quamvis revera Deus ad modum causae Physicae Voluntatem determinet. Exercit. 3. cap. 1.
english: In his Exercitationes apologeticae pro divina gratia Rutherford maintains that in all acts, of nature and of grace alike, God determines the will by a truly real impulse, in the manner of a physical cause. He adds, though, that the main dispute is not whether this predetermination should be called physical, but whether God predetermines free acts in a way that cannot be turned aside.

'The question,' he says, 'is whether God does not so move the will that, under that motion, once moved it cannot fail to be fully moved; or whether God's action on the will does not so bend it that it cannot fail freely to bend itself where God inclines it. We, for our part, prove from Scripture that the will is necessitated by God's motion, by which it is moved beyond turning aside.' If anyone grants this, he adds, he is ready to bid farewell to physical predetermination, although in reality God does determine the will in the manner of a physical cause (Exercitation 3, chapter 1).

source_text: XLIV. Tuissus autem Theologus Anglus distinguit concursum Dei ab ejus praedeterminatione, licet utrumque necessarium putet ad omnes creaturae actiones. Et concursum quidem agnoscit esse simul & natura, & tempore cum operatione creaturae, sed vult ipsi adjunctam esse motionem quandam praeviam in ipsam voluntatem. Etiam concursum, inquit, admittimus simultaneum tam natura quam tempore in actum; sed concursum istum dicimus complicare motionem praeviam in ipsam Voluntatem, praeviam, inquam, non tempore, sed natura. Vindiciarum lib. 2. part. 3. Et in eodem lib. pag. 18. Concursum indifferentem & indeterminatum, qualem Jesuitae docent, his Verbis respuit, Ego vero concursum istum indifferentem atque indefinitum perperam institui tam evidenter demonstrari posse existimo, quam solem meridianum lucere.
english: The English theologian William Twisse distinguishes God's concurrence from his predetermination, though he thinks both necessary for every action of the creature. He grants that the concurrence is simultaneous with the creature's operation in both nature and time, but he insists that it is joined with a certain prior motion on the will itself.

'We too admit a concurrence on the act,' he says, 'simultaneous both in nature and in time; but we say that this concurrence involves a prior motion on the will itself, prior, I mean, not in time but in nature' (Vindiciae, book 2, part 3). In the same book, at page 18, he rejects an indifferent and undetermined concurrence of the kind the Jesuits teach: 'For my part I think it can be shown that this indifferent and indefinite concurrence is wrongly posited, as plainly as that the sun shines at noon.'

source_text: XLV. Caeterum ex rationibus ab Amesio & Retorforti allatis clarum est eos istud praecipue negatum velle, & tanquam maximum errorem abhorrere, quod non alia sit Dei circa creaturam actus operatio & efficacia, quam quae in concursu quodam ex se indifferenti & indefinito consistat. Quod certe minime affirmare intendunt omnes illi qui alioquin generalem Dei concursum, qui ad singulos actus creaturarum necessarius est, statuunt esse ex se indifferentem, & a causis secundis varie determinari. Quippe praeter illum Dei concursum generalem, agnoscunt magnam esse providentiae divinae vim & efficaciam, in variis rerum eventis procurandis, promovendis, moderandis atque dirigendis; & praesertim circa hominum Voluntates, & actus ab illis libere elicitos, quod Strangius multis in locis diligenter observat.
english: From the reasons Ames and Rutherford give, it is clear that what they chiefly mean to deny, and shrink from as the gravest error, is that God's operation and efficacy concerning the creature's act consists in nothing more than a concurrence that is indifferent and indefinite in itself.

Those who otherwise hold that God's general concurrence, needed for each act of creatures, is indifferent in itself and variously determined by secondary causes have no intention whatever of asserting that. Besides that general concurrence of God, they recognize the great power and efficacy of divine providence in bringing about, furthering, regulating and directing all kinds of events, especially where human wills and the acts freely elicited by them are concerned. Strang points this out carefully in many places.

source_text: XLVI. Quod spectat autem conciliationem concursus istius praedeterminantis cum arbitrii libertate, ex mente Amesii dicendum est cum Didaco Alvares praedeterminationem Dei non impedire quominus Voluntas libere agat, quoniam efficit quidem ut Voluntas agat certo & infallibiliter, sed tamen ab ea non tollit potestatem aliter agendi. Et similiter Tuissus dicit, Deum ita movere voluntates hominum ad aliquid agendum, ut quicquid fit, liberae voluntatis ipsorum conditioni convenienter fiat: ita ut in ipso momento quo agunt, possint non agere, nempe in sensu diviso. Nam in sensu composito prorsus ἀδύνατον est.
english: As for reconciling this predetermining concurrence with freedom of choice, on Ames's view one must say with Diego Alvarez that God's predetermination does not prevent the will from acting freely. It does make the will act certainly and infallibly, yet it does not take from the will the power to act otherwise.

Twisse likewise says that God moves human wills to do something in such a way that whatever happens comes about in keeping with the condition of their free will, so that at the very moment they act they are able not to act, in the divided sense, that is. 'In the composite sense it is utterly impossible.'

source_text: XLVII. Juxta Retorfortem vero ad libertatem duplex indifferentia concurrit, una objectiva, quando intellectus proponit aliquod eligibile voluntati, ut medium summo bono absolute intento non necessarium: alia interna, vitalis, electiva, qua voluntas ex se potest tam hoc velle, quam nolle, salva tum essentia libertatis, tum salvo naturalissimo agendi modo suo. Neutri autem indifferentiae Dei praedeterminatio ullatenus praejudicat. Non objectivae, quoniam non impedit quominus intellectus objectum eligibile voluntati proponat, ut idoneum quidem ad finem consequendum, sed tamen non habens cum eo connexionem necessariam. Non etiam internae, quoniam Deus determinans voluntatem ad hoc nolendum, non obstat quominus possit per naturam illud velle. Denique omnes illi Theologi in hoc conveniunt, ex Dei praemotione & praedeterminatione imponi quidem aliquam necessitatem actibus voluntatis, sed necessitatem tantum hypotheticam, quae non pugnat cum libertate, quam evertit sola necessitas a vi externa, aut a naturali determinatione orta.
english: According to Rutherford, two kinds of indifference go to make up freedom. One is objective: the intellect puts before the will something it may choose, as a means that is not necessary to the highest good intended absolutely. The other is internal, vital and elective: by it the will of itself is able as much to will a thing as to refuse it, with both the essence of freedom and its own most natural way of acting kept intact.

God's predetermination prejudices neither kind of indifference in any way. Not the objective kind, since it does not prevent the intellect from setting before the will an object it may choose, one suited to reaching the end but not necessarily connected with it. Nor the internal kind, since when God determines the will to refuse this, he does not stand in the way of its being able by nature to will it.

Finally, all these theologians agree that God's premotion and predetermination does impose some necessity on the acts of the will, but only a hypothetical necessity. That does not conflict with freedom, which is overturned only by necessity arising from external force or from natural determination.

source_text: XLVIII. Non desunt etiam inter Scholae Reformatae Doctores qui circa Dei generalem concursum ad omnes creaturarum actus necessarium, idem sentire videntur cum Durando, & Ludovico a Dola, Scholae Romanae Doctoribus. Nam vir Clarissimus Moses Amyraldus non videtur alium concursum Dei generalem, quo cum causis omnibus secundis concurrat, agnoscere, praeter continuam illam efficaciam, qua rei cujusque naturam, & vires ei a natura concessas tuetur & sustentat. Unde colligit concursum illum ad libertatem nihil attinere. Fac enim, inquit, naturam & ejus vires consistere posse citra opem talis concursus, operabuntur illae certe libere. Accedat ergo concursus qui nihil aliud praestat, quam ut quae alioqui conciderent, atque evanescerent, in statu naturali consistant & conserventur, libertas inde nihil detrimenti capiet. Quae verba satis indicant, hac in parte, Virum Clarissimum idem, ut jam dictum, cum Durando veteri Scholastico sentire. De libero Arbitrio cap. 4. sub finem.
english: Among the teachers of the Reformed School there are also some who, regarding God's general concurrence needed for every act of creatures, seem to think as Durandus and Louis of Dole, teachers of the Roman School, do.

The distinguished Moïse Amyraut, for instance, seems to recognize no general concurrence of God, by which he concurs with all secondary causes, beyond the continual efficacy by which he keeps and sustains the nature of each thing and the powers nature has given it. From this he concludes that such concurrence has no bearing on freedom. 'Suppose,' he says, 'that nature and its powers could subsist without the help of such concurrence; they will certainly act freely. Now add a concurrence that does nothing more than keep in their natural state, and preserve, things that would otherwise collapse and vanish: freedom will suffer no harm from it.' These words show clearly enough that on this point the distinguished author holds, as already said, the same view as the old scholastic Durandus (De libero arbitrio, chapter 4, near the end).

source_text: XLIX. Veruntamen praeter istum concursum generalem agnoscit magnam esse providentiae Dei efficaciam, qua actus voluntatis nostrae tam bonos, quam malos & indifferentes, conformiter suo aeterno decreto in tempore determinat. Sed totam illam divinae providentiae efficacitatem, quae sese in bono exerit, reducit ad duos actus, nempe ad objecti propositionem, quam libertatem nihil violare manifestum est. Deinde ad internam subjecti dispositionem, quae in eo consistit, ut facultates liberentur ab impedimentis, quae ad nativam eorum constitutionem accesserunt, aut etiam supra naturae sortem aliquo modo evehantur, qua in re non minus evidens est hominis libertati nihil praejudicari.
english: Even so, besides that general concurrence Amyraut recognizes a great efficacy of God's providence, by which God determines in time the acts of our will, good, bad and indifferent alike, in keeping with his eternal decree.

But he reduces the whole efficacy of divine providence that shows itself in good acts to two operations. The first is the presenting of the object, which plainly does no violence to freedom. The second is the inner disposing of the subject, which consists in freeing the faculties from the hindrances that have come upon their native constitution, or even in raising them in some way above the lot of nature. Here too it is no less evident that human freedom suffers no prejudice.

source_text: L. Similiter quoad actus malos, circa eos docet esse duplicem Providentiae actum, unum externum, & alterum internum. Et externum quidem dicit circa duo occupari. Vel enim, inquit, versatur in propositione objectorum, quae facultates commovere idonea sunt: Vel in eo consistit, quod Deus nihil agit quidem, sed sinit & patitur Diabolum ἐνέργειαν suam explicare, ut objectorum efficacitatem adjuvet. Internus autem Dei actus, qui in malis hominum operibus intervenit, in eo juxta ipsum consistit, quod Deus ex pluribus objectis ad malum inducentibus, quae homo in mente agitat, unum vel obscurat, vel omnino ex mente eripit, aut etiam unum aliquod objectum ab ea parte offerri procurat, qua est maxime aptum, & idoneum ad movendum. In quibus omnibus pariter nihil potest officere humanae libertati.
english: In the same way, with respect to evil acts, he teaches that Providence acts in two ways, one external and the other internal. The external act, he says, concerns two things. 'Either it is engaged in presenting objects fitted to stir the faculties, or it consists in this: God does nothing himself, but allows and permits the devil to exercise his working, so as to add to the force of the objects.'

God's internal act in the evil deeds of human beings consists, according to him, in this: out of the many objects leading to evil that a person turns over in his mind, God either obscures one or removes it from the mind altogether, or else arranges for some one object to be presented from the side on which it is most apt and suited to move. In none of this, likewise, can there be anything harmful to human freedom.

source_text: LI. Denique circa actus indifferentes efficaciam Dei eodem modo revocat ad objectorum propositionem, administrationem causarum quae objecta juvare possunt, & internam operationem, quae facit ut unum objectum alteri praevaleat, & eo modo menti se offerat, qua aptum est illam commovere. Et tamen per istas operationes, quae ex omnium confessione, libertatem nihil laedunt, vult omnes humanos actus efficaciter a Deo determinari, & certissime aeterna decreta Dei de illis adimpleri; quia scilicet, facultates humanae, nempe mens & Voluntas, ad certas actiones determinantur ab objectis, quae illis proponuntur congruenter & consentanee illarum affectioni & dispositioni. Unde oritur quaedam in operationibus earum necessitas, quae cum libertate optime consentit; & sufficit tamen, ut quae Deus in aeterno suo consilio certissime designavit, & fienda determinavit, ab hominibus certissime pariter & indeclinabiliter peragantur.
english: Finally, for indifferent acts he traces God's efficacy in the same way to three things: the presenting of objects, the management of causes that can lend those objects force, and an inner operation that makes one object prevail over another and present itself to the mind in the way best suited to move it.

Yet through these operations, which by everyone's admission do no harm to freedom, he holds that all human acts are efficaciously determined by God and that God's eternal decrees about them are fulfilled with complete certainty. The reason is that the human faculties, mind and will, are determined to particular actions by the objects set before them in a way that fits their inclination and disposition. From this arises a kind of necessity in their operations which agrees perfectly well with freedom, and which is still enough to ensure that what God has most surely planned in his eternal counsel and determined shall be done is carried out by human beings with equal certainty and without swerving.

source_text: LII. Josue Placeus vero Theologus Doctissimus, atque subtilissimus, cum Theologis reliquis, agnoscit quidem voluntatem in agendo, ut alias causas secundas, a Deo dependere, tanquam a prima causa; quae autem & quanta sit illa dependentia, pro sua modestia definire non audet, nec vult judicium suum interponere super variis illis quaestionibus, quae de Dei concursu, & cooperatione cum omnibus causis secundis in Scholis agitari solent. Haec enim sunt illius verba, Voluntas pendet a Deo, ut a prima causa, a qua causae secundae omnes in agendo dependent. Quanta autem sit causarum secundarum in causando dependentia a prima causa, disputatur acriter inter Pontificios. Concurrere quidem cum omni causa, ut convenienter facultatibus suis operetur, in confesso est apud omnes. Sed hunc concursum pleriq; omnes immediatum, proximum, ac eundem plane cum ipsa actione causarum secundarum esse contendunt, aliis quibusdam reclamantibus. Deque illo ipso concursu immediato inter se obnixe totis viribus Dominicani, & Jesuitae digladiantur: illis pro Physica quam vocant praedeterminatione, his contra illam fortiter pugnantibus. Nos quidem qua reverentia erga infinitam Dei majestatem ducimur, non audemus definire quanta sit dependentia causae secundae a prima. Nobis sufficit, modo ne Deo ullam peccatorum nostrorum vel minimam labem aspergat, non posse nimiam statui. Tractatu de liber. Arbitr. p. 174.
english: Josué de la Place, a most learned and very subtle theologian, agrees with the other theologians that the will in acting depends on God as on the first cause, as other secondary causes do. But being a modest man he does not venture to define what that dependence is or how great it is, and he declines to give his judgment on the various questions about God's concurrence and cooperation with all secondary causes that are commonly debated in the Schools.

These are his words: 'The will depends on God as on the first cause, on which all secondary causes depend in acting. How far secondary causes depend on the first cause in their causing is fiercely disputed among the papists. That God concurs with every cause, so that it acts in keeping with its faculties, is admitted by all. But nearly all of them maintain that this concurrence is immediate, proximate, and simply the same as the action of the secondary causes themselves, though some others object. And over that very immediate concurrence the Dominicans and the Jesuits fight each other stubbornly with all their might, the former for what they call physical predetermination, the latter strenuously opposing it. For our part, out of the reverence we owe to God's infinite majesty, we do not venture to define how great the dependence of the secondary cause on the first is. It is enough for us that, provided it does not cast on God even the slightest stain of our sins, it cannot be made too great' (Treatise on free choice, p. 174).

source_text: LIII. Istam vero voluntatis a prima causa dependentiam, sic, paucis interjectis, cum ejusdem voluntatis libertate conciliat. Quomodocunque autem Voluntas nostra pendeat a Deo, ac quicquid in ea Deus operetur, constat semper illi libertas ea quam in immunitate a triplici necessitate, coactionis, determinationis a materia, & determinationis a sensu positam esse diximus.
english: A little further on he reconciles this dependence of the will on the first cause with the will's freedom. He writes:

'However our will may depend on God, and whatever God may work in it, it always keeps the freedom that we said lies in exemption from a threefold necessity: of coercion, of determination by matter, and of determination by the senses.'

source_text: LIV. Nec multum absimilis est Paraei sententia. Damnat enim temeritatem Doctorum Scholasticorum varias quaestiones circa Dei concursum moventium & determinantium, Quis, inquit, temeraria curiositate investigare, & definire sunt ausi quod sciri & explicari satis non potest. Sententiam vero Cajetani, cui Concordia Liberi Arbitrii cum divina Providentia videtur inexplicabilis, & non intelligibilis in hac vita, judicat esse tutissimam, quia judicia Dei sunt inscrutabilia, & viae ejus impervestigabiles. In genere solum vult hoc pro certo haberi, hominis voluntatem Dei nutu regi, & quo vult inclinari. Ut vero illud cum nostra libertate conciliet, dicit illud non agere libere quod aliunde regitur sine deliberatione & electione propria. Quod vero Deus regit monstrans intellectui objectum, & eo efficaciter movens & afficiens Voluntatem, ad hoc vel illud sponte eligendum, id nihilominus libere eligere, etsi nutu Dei quo ipse vult inclinetur: Sicut, inquit, exempli causa, tyro litteras pingere discens libere scribit, licet manus ejus a Paedagogo regatur. Et huc etiam respicit quod addit paulo post, & saepe repetit, Deum concursu suo quidem determinare voluntatem humanam, sed non determinatione Physica, bruta, violenta, verum spontanea cum judicio proprio, & electione conjuncta. Animadversionibus in Bellarmini librum quartum de lib. Arbitr. cap. 14.
english: Pareus's view is not very different. He condemns the rashness of the scholastic teachers who raise and settle various questions about God's concurrence, 'in which', he says, 'they have dared with rash curiosity to investigate and define what cannot be adequately known or explained.' He judges safest the view of Cajetan, who found the agreement of free choice with divine providence inexplicable and beyond understanding in this life, because God's judgments are unsearchable and his ways past finding out.

In general he wants only this held as certain: that the human will is governed by God's nod and inclined wherever he wills. To reconcile this with our freedom, he says that what is governed from outside, without its own deliberation and choice, does not act freely. But when God governs by showing the intellect an object, and through it efficaciously moving and affecting the will to choose this or that of its own accord, the will still chooses freely, even though it is inclined by God's nod wherever he wills. 'In the same way,' he says, 'a beginner learning to form his letters writes freely, though his hand is guided by the schoolmaster.'

This is also the point of what he adds a little later and often repeats: that God by his concurrence does determine the human will, 'but not by a physical, brute, violent determination; rather by a spontaneous one, joined with its own judgment and choice' (Animadversions on Bellarmine's fourth book on free choice, chapter 14).

source_text: LV. Quantum ad me attinet, horumce Doctissimorum Virorum modestiam maxime laudandam censeo: & modum divini concursus, quo cum causis secundis prima cooperatur, pro certo definire mihi temerarium & nimium audax videtur, cum ingenii nostri tenuitas divinae potentiae, & sapientiae abyssum penetrare & scrutari non valeat: nec ea res sit satis ratione percepta, aut sat distincte in sacra Scriptura revelata.
english: For my part, I think the modesty of these very learned men deserves the highest praise. To define with certainty the manner of divine concurrence by which the first cause cooperates with secondary causes seems to me rash and far too bold.
Our feeble understanding cannot penetrate and search out the abyss of God's power and wisdom, and the matter is neither adequately grasped by reason nor revealed clearly enough in Holy Scripture.

source_text: LVI. In primis autem percipere non possum quomodo statui possit, Deum causas liberas, etiam ad actus intrinsece malos Physice praemovere, & praedeterminare, quin inde sequatur Deum esse peccati authorem. Quis enim capiat, exempli gratia, Deum influxu quodam omnem humanae voluntatis motum antecedente, imposuisse primo homini necessitatem fructum vetitum appetendi, & appetitum comedendi: atque etiam quotidie efficientia quadam proprie dicta, homines praedeterminare, & ut sic barbare loquar necessitare ad hoc ut Deum blasphement, & eum odio habeant; & tamen culpam, quae ab istis actibus separari non potest, in Deum ipsum refundendam non esse?
english: Above all, I cannot see how anyone can hold that God physically premoves and predetermines free causes even to acts that are intrinsically evil without its following that God is the author of sin.

Who could understand, for instance, that God, by an influence preceding every motion of the human will, laid on the first man a necessity of desiring the forbidden fruit and an appetite for eating it; and that every day, by an efficient causality in the proper sense, he predetermines people, and, to use a barbarous word, 'necessitates' them to blaspheme God and hate him; and yet that the guilt, which cannot be separated from those acts, is not to be laid back on God himself?

source_text: LVII. Sed modo Deus author peccati non constituatur, cum Doctissimo Placeo, judico causarum secundarum in agendo dependentiam a prima nimiam statui non posse. Et maxime quoque mihi probabile videtur Deum, juxta communem Scholarum sententiam, ad omnes & singulos creaturarum actus immediate concurrere.
english: But as long as God is not made the author of sin, I judge with the most learned de la Place that the dependence of secondary causes on the first in their acting cannot be made too great.
It also seems to me highly probable that God, as the Schools commonly hold, concurs immediately in each and every act of creatures.

source_text: LVIII. Praesertim autem illud mihi certissimum est, quod etiam ab omnibus Theologis concedi puto, divinae providentiae vim & efficaciam, etiam circa actus malos, minime restringendam esse ad concursum quendam ex se generalem & indifferentem; sed Deum multis modis sapientiae ipsius cognitis, varios rerum eventus, etiam in quibus hominum malitia intervenit, procurare, promovere, dirigere atque moderari.
english: What I hold as most certain of all, and what I think all theologians grant, is that the power and efficacy of divine providence, even in regard to evil acts, must in no way be confined to a concurrence that is general and indifferent in itself.
In many ways known to his own wisdom, God brings about, furthers, directs and regulates the varied course of events, including those in which human wickedness plays a part.

source_text: LIX. Nec minus apud me certum est, quocunque modo Deus in causis liberis agat & operetur, id facere semper ipsarum naturae congruenter, nec quicquam libertati earum praejudicare: ac proinde quum voluntates humanas ad hunc aut illum actum efficaciter movet, ab iis non tollere potestatem aliter agendi.
english: I am no less certain that, in whatever way God acts and works in free causes, he always does so in keeping with their nature and without any prejudice to their freedom.
So when he efficaciously moves human wills to one act or another, he does not take from them the power to act otherwise.
